[[File:Matrix Signal-Flow Graph.png|thumb|A multi-input, multi-output system represented as a noncommutative matrix signal-flow graph.]]

In [[automata theory]] and [[control theory]], branches of [[mathematics]], [[theoretical computer science]] and [[systems engineering]], a '''noncommutative signal-flow graph''' is a tool for modeling{{sfn|Lorens|1964}} interconnected systems and state machines by mapping the edges of a [[directed graph]] to a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] or [[semiring]].

A single edge '''weight''' might represent an array of [[impulse response]]s of a complex system (see figure to the right),{{sfn|Riegle|Lin|1972}} or a character from an [[Alphabet (computer science)|alphabet]] picked off the [[Finite state transducer|input tape]] of a finite automaton,{{sfn|Brzozowski|McCluskey|1963}} while the graph might represent the flow of information or state transitions.

As diverse as these applications are, they share much of the same underlying theory.{{sfn|Book|Even|Greibach|Ott|1971}}{{sfn|Pliam|Lee|1995}}

==Definition==
[[File:Signal-Flow Graph Fragment.png|thumb|Signal-flow graph fragment.]]

{{confusing|reason=what is defined here, in terms of what?|date=September 2015}}
Consider ''n'' equations involving ''n''+1 variables {''x''<sub>0</sub>, ''x''<sub>1</sub>,...,''x''<sub>n</sub>}.

:<math>x_i = \sum_{j=0}^n a_{ij}x_j, \;\;\; 1\leq i \leq n,</math>

with ''a''<sub>ij</sub> elements in a ring or semiring ''R''.  The free variable ''x''<sub>0</sub> corresponds to a source vertex ''v''<sub>0</sub>, thus having no defining equation.  Each equation corresponds to a fragment of a [[directed graph]] ''G''=(''V'',''E'') as show in the figure.

The edge weights define a function ''f'' from ''E'' to ''R''.  Finally fix an output vertex ''v<sub>m</sub>''.  A signal-flow graph is the collection of this data ''S'' = (''G''=(''V'',''E''), ''v<sub>0</sub>'',''v<sub>m</sub>'' <math>\in</math> ''V'', ''f'' : ''E'' → ''R'').  The equations may not have a solution, but when they do,

:<math>x_m = T x_0,</math>

with ''T'' an element of ''R'' called the '''gain'''.

==Return Loop Method==
There exist several{{sfn|Riegle|Lin|1972}} noncommutative generalizations of [[Mason's rule]].{{clarify|reason=Mason's rule should have been introduced before here.|date=September 2015}} The most common is the  '''return loop method''' (sometimes called the '''forward return loop method (FRL)''', having a dual '''backward return loop method (BRL)''').  The first rigorous proof{{clarify|Which property (of the return loop method?) has been proven?|date=September 2015}} is attributed to Riegle,{{sfn|Riegle|Lin|1972}} so it is sometimes called '''Riegle's rule'''.{{sfn|Andaloussi|Chalh|Sueur|2006|pp=2962}}

As with [[Mason's rule]], these{{clarify|reason=which?|date=September 2015}} gain expressions combine terms in a [[graph-theoretic]] manner (loop-gains, path products, etc.).  They are known to hold over an arbitrary [[noncommutative ring]] and over the [[semiring]] of regular expressions.{{sfn|Pliam|Lee|1995}}

===Formal Description===
The method{{clarify|reason=which one? Mason's? FRL? BRL?|date=September 2015}} starts by enumerating all paths from input to output,{{clarify|reason=i/o of what? Does the method start of a directed graph with a given input and a given output node?|date=September 2015}} indexed by ''j'' <math>\in</math> ''J''.  We use the following definitions:

* The ''j''-th '''path product''' is (by abuse of notation) a [[tuple]] of ''k<sub>j</sub>'' edge weights along it:

::::<math>p_j = (w^{(j)}_{k_j},\ldots, w^{(j)}_2, w^{(j)}_1).</math>{{clarify|reason=what is w^(j)_i ?|date=September 2015}}

* To '''split''' a vertex ''v'' is to replace it with a source and sink respecting the original incidence and weights (this is the inverse of the graph morphism taking source and sink to ''v'').
* The '''[[loop gain]]''' of a vertex ''v'' w.r.t. a subgraph ''H'' is the gain from source to sink of the signal-flow graph split at ''v'' after removing all vertices not in ''H''.
* Each path defines an ordering of vertices along it. The along path ''j'', the ''i''-th '''FRL (BRL) node factor''' is (1-''S<sub>i</sub><sup>(j)</sup>'')<sup>−1</sup> where ''S<sub>i</sub><sup>(j)</sup>'' is the loop gain of the ''i''-th vertex along the ''j''-th w.r.t. the subgraph obtained by removing ''v''<sub>0</sub> and all vertices ahead of (behind) it.

The contribution of the ''j''-th path to the gain is the product along the path, alternating between the path product weights 
and the node factors:

:<math>T_j = \prod_{i=k_j}^1 (1-S^{(j)}_i)^{-1} w^{(j)}_i,</math>

so the total gain is

:<math>T = \sum_{j\in J} T_j.</math>

===An Example===
[[File:FRL BRL Example.png|thumb|A noncommutative signal-flow graph from ''x'' to ''z'']]

Consider the [[signal-flow graph]] shown.  From ''x'' to ''z'', there are two path products: (''d'') and (''e,a'').  Along (''d''), the FRL and BRL contributions coincide as both share same loop gain (whose split reappears in the upper right of the table below):

:<math>f+e(1-b)^{-1}c,</math>

Multiplying its node factor and path weight, its gain contribution is

:<math>T_d = \left[1 - f - e(1-b)^{-1}c \right]^{-1}d.</math>

Along path (''e,a''), FRL and BRL differ slightly, each having distinct splits of vertices ''y'' and ''z'' as shown in the following table.

:[[File:Return Loop Split Table.png|540px]]

Adding to ''T<sub>d</sub>'', the alternating product of node factors and path weights, we obtain two gain expressions:

:<math>T^{(FRL)} = \left[1 - f - e(1-b)^{-1}c \right]^{-1}d  + \left[1 - f - e(1-b)^{-1}c \right]^{-1}e(1-b)^{-1}a,</math>

and

:<math>T^{(BRL)} = \left[1 - f - e(1-b)^{-1}c \right]^{-1}d + (1-f)^{-1}e\left[1 - b - c(1-f)^e\right]^{-1}a,</math>

These values are easily seen to be the same using identities (''ab'')<sup>−1</sup> = ''b''<sup>−1</sup>''a''<sup>−1</sup> and ''a''(1-''ba'')<sup>−1</sup>=(1-''ab'')<sup>−1</sup>''a''.

==Applications==

===Matrix Signal-Flow Graphs===
Consider equations

:<math>y_i=\sum_{j=1}^2 a_{ij} x_j + \sum_{j=1}^2 b_{ij}y_j</math>

and

:<math>z_i=\sum_{j=1}^2 c_{ij} y_j,</math>

This system could be modeled as scalar signal-flow graph with multiple inputs and outputs.  But, the variables naturally fall into layers, which can be collected into vectors 
''x''=(''x''<sub>1</sub>,''x''<sub>2</sub>)<sup>''t''</sup>
''y''=(''y''<sub>1</sub>,''y''<sub>2</sub>)<sup>''t''</sup> and
''z''=(''z''<sub>1</sub>,''z''<sub>2</sub>)<sup>''t''</sup>.
This results in much simpler '''matrix signal-flow graph''' as shown in the figure at the top of the article.

Applying the forward return loop method is trivial as there's a single path product (''C'',''A'') with a single loop-gain ''B'' at ''y''.  Thus as a matrix, this system has a very compact representation of its input-output map:

:<math>T = C(1-B)^{-1}A.</math>

===Finite Automata===
[[File:Automaton as Signal-Flow Graph.png|thumb|Representation of a finite automaton as a (noncommutative) signal flow graph over a semiring.]]

An important kind of noncommutative signal-flow graph is a [[Finite-state machine|finite state]] [[automaton]] over an alphabet <math>\Sigma</math>.{{sfn|Brzozowski|McCluskey|1963}}{{sfn|Book|Even|Greibach|Ott|1971}}

Serial connections correspond to the concatenation of words, which can be extended to subsets of the [[free monoid]] <math>\Sigma^*</math>. For ''A'', ''B'' <math>\subseteq\Sigma^*</math>

:<math>A \cdot B = \{ab \mid a\in A, b\in B\}.</math>

Parallel connections correspond to [[set union]], which in this context is often written ''A''+''B''.

Finally, self-loops naturally correspond to the [[Kleene closure]]

:<math>A^* = \{\lambda\} + A + AA + AAA + \cdots,</math>

where <math>\lambda</math> is the [[empty word]]. The similarity to the infinite geometric series

:<math>(1-x)^{-1} = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 \cdots,</math>

is more than superficial, as expressions of this form serve as 'inversion' in this [[semiring]].{{sfn|Kuich|Salomaa|1985}}

In this way, the subsets of <math>\Sigma^*</math> built of from finitely many of these three operations can be identified with the [[semiring]] of [[regular expressions]].  Similarly, finite graphs whose edges are weighted by subsets of <math>\Sigma^*</math> can be identified with finite automata, though generally that theory starts with [[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] sets as in the figure.

This automaton is deterministic so we can unambiguously enumerate paths via words. Using the return loop method, path contributions are:

* path ''ab'', has node factors (''c''<sup>*</sup>, <math>\lambda</math>), yielding gain contribution

::<math>ac^*b,</math>

* path ''ada'', has node factors (''c''<sup>*</sup>, ''c''<sup>*</sup>, <math>\lambda</math>), yielding gain contribution

::<math>ac^*dc^*a,</math>

* path ''ba'', has node factors (''c''<sup>*</sup>, <math>\lambda</math>), yielding gain contribution

::<math>bc^*a.</math>

Thus the [[Formal language|language]] accepted by this automaton (the gain of its signal-flow graph) is the sum of these terms

:<math>L = ac^*b+ac^*dc^*a+bc^*a.</math>
